column6: I and II are TRUE and III and IV are FALSE.

title: Which of the following statements is TRUE?
Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery Final Exam: It is not necessary to provide any information to an Oral and Maxillofacial Pathologist about a lesion or patient, because a good Oral and Maxillofacial Pathologist only cares about what she/he sees when looking at a specimen under the microscope.

final: A general pathologist can make as accurate a diagnosis of odontogenic lesions as an Oral and Maxillofacial Pathologist.
column5: If a dentist advises a patient of the need for biopsy of a potentially dangerous oral lesion and the patient does not follow-up, the dentist bears no responsibility to attempt to have the patient obtain treatment.
column6: If you observe a lesion whose appearance is highly suspicious of malignancy and the specimen is read as benign, you do not need to re-evaluate or follow the lesion.

title: Which of the following statements about cystic lesions is FALSE?
Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery Final Exam: Enucleation of a cystic lesion is often performed as an excisional biopsy and no further treatment is necessary.

column6: Once marsupialization of a cystic lesion is performed, no further treatment will be necessary.

title: Consider the following statements. I. The sublingual space is located inferior to the mylohyoid muscle. II. title: Which of the following statements regarding incision and drainage procedures is FALSE?

title: A 26 year-old male was playing hockey without a proper mask and was hit in the mouth with a puck. On examination, teeth 4, 5, and 6 have mobility, moving together when any of the teeth are pushed individually. They are NOT separately mobile and move almost as an entire segment. The remainder of the oral/dental examination is within normal limits. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery Final Exam: You diagnose this as luxation of teeth 4, 5, 6 and place a semi-rigid composite splint.
omfs: You diagnose this as an alveolar fracture, digitally reduce the segment and check occlusion. Then you place a rigid splint for fixation.
final: You diagnose this as luxation of teeth 4, 5, 6 and an alveolar fracture so you place a composite splint spanning across teeth 2-8 and a rigid splint from 2-15.
column5: You diagnose this as intrusion and luxation of teeth 4, 5, 6 and place a composite semi-rigid splint across teeth 4, 5, 6.

column6: Where were you going when this occurred?

title: Which of the following statements is TRUE?

title: A 46 year-old female presents to your office for extraction of tooth 12. It was previously endodontically treated with post/core and pfm crown. The pfm crown has fractured and is loosely attached to the remainder of the tooth root. The tooth also has a periapical radiolucent lesion with an associated draining fistula on the palate. You attempt to extract the tooth surgically – raising a flap and using a handpiece to trough the buccal aspect and find a purchase. However, the tooth continues to fracture until you have less than 2mm of the dilacerated palatal root remaining. Note that the tooth apex is not proximal to the maxillary sinus. What is your next step?

omfs: Leave the root in place to avoid any further complications.
final: Tell the patient that you are going to leave the root fragment in place today and retrieve it in another 6 months once it has erupted more
column5: Drill as much of the tooth root down so that it is less than 1mm in size, and then it is okay to leave it.

title: You are extracting stand-alone, erupted tooth 16 on a 59 year-old male. You administer local anesthesia and begin to gently elevate the tooth. While you are elevating the tooth, you hear a loud crack. What do you do next?
Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery Final Exam: Continue to elevate and extract the tooth. A crack is part of the normal sounds you would hear when extracting any tooth.
omfs: Check to see if the maxillary tuberosity is still intact. If it has fractured, you just continue to perform the extraction as usual and just remove it if it comes with the tooth.
final: Check to see if the maxillary tuberosity is still intact. If it has fractured, you gently dissect the soft tissue off around it and deliver it with the tooth atraumatically. You then smooth any sharp bony ridges and suture any mucosal tears.
column5: Check to see if there’s an oral antral communication. If there is, you continue to extract the tooth as you usually would and leave the socket open to heal by secondary intention.

title: A 78 year-old male presents for extraction of stand-alone tooth 2. The sinus is severely pneumatized on both the distal and mesial aspects. You perform the extraction surgically, raising a flap and using a surgical handpiece.  However, you realize that an oral antral communication occurs and you treat it correctly, as follows:

final: The oral antral communication is >6mm, so you perform a tension free primary closure and instruct the patient to follow strict sinus precautions for the following 6-8 weeks.
column5: The oral antral communication is <2mm, so you do not suture it but you do instruct the patient to follow strict sinus precautions for the following 6-8 weeks.
column6: The oral antral communication is 3-6mm, so you don’t tell the patient and if he notices it later, you tell him it was his fault for not following the post-op instructions.
